**Amanda Stern** is an American writer and literary event organizer. She has written under the [pen names](link_6)**A.****J. Stern** and **Fiona Rosenbloom**.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amanda_Stern&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

When she was a senior in high school, at [Friends Seminary](link_7),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-TheNewYorker-1) Stern starred in an [off-Broadway](link_8) production of _Sometimes I Wake Up in the Middle of the Night_, a play she co-wrote.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-TheNewYorker-1) From there she turned to film, working for [Good Machine](link_9), [Hal Hartley](link_10), [Ang Lee](link_11) and [Terry Gilliam](link_12). She also worked as a comic, co-hosting the [Lorne Michaels](link_13) comedy series "This is Not a Test" alongside [Marc Maron](link_14) at [Catch a Rising Star](link_15). Soon after, she became an on-air host for Lorne Michaels' [Burly Bear Network](link_16).

In 2003, Stern founded [The Happy Ending Music and Reading Series](link_3), which was cited by local critics as one of the best authors' series in New York City.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-4) In 2006, she was profiled in the "New York" issue of _[The New York Times Magazine](link_17)_ as one of ten "New Bohemians, helping to keep downtown New York alive".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-5) In January 2009, the series moved to uptown to [Joe's Pub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe [link_18]'s_Pub "Joe's Pub") at the [Public Theater](link_19). The last event was held in May 2016.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-7)

Stern has written eleven books for children under the pseudonyms A. J. Stern and Fiona Rosenbloom.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-8) Her debut novel, _The Long Haul_, was well-received by _[SFGate](link_20)_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-9) Her 2005 young-adult novel (authored with Rosenbloom pseudonym) _You are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah_ was turned into a 2023 [movie of the same title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah "You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah") starring [Adam Sandler](link_21).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-TheNewYorker-1)

Stern has held several residencies at [Yaddo](link_22) and [MacDowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacDowell_(artists [link_23]'_residency_and_workshop) "MacDowell (artists' residency and workshop)"). She lives in [Fort Greene, Brooklyn](link_24).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern#cite_note-10)

_**You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah**_ is a 2023 American [coming-of-age](link_21)[comedy-drama](link_22) film directed by [Sammi Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen "Sammi Cohen"), written by Alison Peck, and produced by [Adam Sandler](link_3), [Tim Herlihy](link_4), [Leslie Morgenstein](link_5), and [Elysa Koplovitz Dutton](link_6). Based on the 2005 [young adult novel](link_23) of the same name, the film stars Sandler and his wife, Jackie Sandler, as well as their daughters, [Sadie](link_10) and [Sunny Sandler](link_8). It also stars [Samantha Lorraine](link_11), [Idina Menzel](link_7), Dylan Hoffman, [Sarah Sherman](link_12), Dan Bulla, [Ido Mosseri](link_13), [Jackie Hoffman](link_14), and [Luis Guzmán](link_15). It tells the story of two best friends whose [bat mitzvah](link_24) plans go awry as they fight for the attention of the same popular boy.

Produced by [Happy Madison Productions](link_18) and [Alloy Entertainment](link_19), the film was released by [Netflix](link_20) on August 25, 2023.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah#cite_note-2)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Stacy Friedman dreams about her upcoming _[bat mitzvah](link_24)_, including sharing it with her best friend Lydia Rodriguez Katz, and sharing a dance with her crush, Andy Goldfarb. She clashes with her parents, Bree and Danny, over planning the "perfect" party, which she believes will determine her future.

When popular student Kym Chang Cohen invites Lydia to her house, Stacy tags along. The girls go on a high ledge, where Andy and his friends meet up with them. On a dare and to impress Andy, Stacy agrees to jump off the ledge into the water below. Enjoying Andy's and everyone's approval is short-lived, as Stacy's bloody maxi-pad floats up next to her. Angry that everyone, including Lydia, is laughing at her, Stacy "calls it", and Lydia announces the time that she lost her crush on Andy.

Once school starts, Stacy learns that Lydia and Andy are dating. Feeling betrayed, she stops talking to her and sends a text message to an anonymous group that Lydia has long hair on her nipples. # Christine Little

Actor, Director, Writer

Christine Little is a Los Angeles-based comic/writer. Little has been on FOX's "Laughs" multiple times, has performed at comedy festivals all over the country such as Limestone, Laughing Skull, Cape Fear and Laugh Your Asheville Off, and opened for headliners such as Mad TV's Bobby Lee. She's also been featured on the front page of Funny or Die, The Huffington Post, as well as in Voyage L.A. Christine has also made appearances on Free Form's "Alone Together" and Comedy Central's "Corporate". She attended the American Academy of Dramatic Arts.

**Elysa Koplovitz Dutton** is a film producer and production executive.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-deadline-1) She is the author[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-2) of the [Penguin/Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Random_House "Penguin Random House") children's book _Christmas Forever: Escape to the North Pole_, illustrated by Manu Montoya, which published in October 2024.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elysa_Dutton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Koplovitz Dutton graduated from [Brown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University") with a bachelor of arts in Art/Semiotics. While at Brown University, she co-created and produced a bi-weekly television soap opera about student life called _Sob Story_ that was nationally syndicated to colleges around the country.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-deadline-1)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elysa_Dutton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Koplovitz Dutton's productions credits with Alloy include [_Purple Hearts_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Hearts_(2022_film) "Purple Hearts (2022 film)"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-5)_[You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You\_Are\_So\_Not\_Invited\_to\_My\_Bat\_Mitzvah "You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah")_,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-6)[_Work It_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_It_(film) "Work It (film)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-7)_[The Sun Is Also a Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sun\_Is\_Also\_a\_Star "The Sun Is Also a Star"),_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-8) and _[Everything, Everything](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everything,\_Everything\_(film) "Everything, Everything (film)")._[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-9) The latter won the [Teen Choice Award for Choice Movie Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_Choice_Award_for_Choice_Movie_-_Drama "Teen Choice Award for Choice Movie - Drama").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-10)

Prior to Alloy, Koplovitz Dutton produced _[Idiocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idiocracy "Idiocracy")_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-11) and _[Like Mike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like\_Mike "Like Mike")._[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton#cite_note-12)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American film director and screenwriter

| Jeremy Garelick |
| --- |
| [![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Jeremy_Garelick.png/250px-Jeremy_Garelick.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeremy_Garelick.png) |
| Born | (1975-11-30) November 30, 1975 (age 50) [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), U.S. |
| Education | [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") |
| Occupations | Screenwriter, film director |
| Years active | 2000–present |

**Jeremy Garelick** (born November 30, 1975) is an American screenwriter, director, and producer.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Garelick&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Garelick was born in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). He attended [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") and graduated in Film Studies.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-1) He is of [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") background.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-2)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Garelick&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After graduating from college, Garelick began his career working as an assistant in [Creative Artists Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Artists_Agency "Creative Artists Agency")'s Motion Picture Literary department. He served as the assistant to director [Joel Schumacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Schumacher "Joel Schumacher") on _[Tigerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigerland "Tigerland")_, _[Bad Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad\_Company\_(2002\_film) "Bad Company (2002 film)")_, _[Phone Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phone\_Booth\_(film) "Phone Booth (film)")_, and _[The Phantom of the Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phantom\_of\_the\_Opera\_(2004\_film) "The Phantom of the Opera (2004 film)")_. He was the second unit director on Schumacher’s 2003 movie _[\_Veronica Guerin\_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veronica\_Guerin\_(film) "Veronica Guerin (film)")_.

While working on Veronica Guerin in 2002, Garelick sold _The Golden Tux_, a spec script he co-wrote with Todd Phillips, to [Dimension Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_Films "Dimension Films"). The script caught the attention of [Vince Vaughn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Vaughn "Vince Vaughn"), who brought Garelick in to co-write and co-produce _[The Break-Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Break-Up "The Break-Up")_.

After the commercial success of _The Break-Up_, Garelick worked with Phillips again on an uncredited re-write of _[The Hangover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hangover "The Hangover")_. The film was a major critical and commercial success, making over $465 million at the box office.

Garelick’s early career came full circle in 2013, when he was hired by [Screen Gems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Gems "Screen Gems") to direct and produce _[The Wedding Ringer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wedding\_Ringer "The Wedding Ringer")_, a feature film that evolved from _The Golden Tux_. Despite negative critical reviews, the film was a box-office success when it premiered in 2015, grossing over $79 million worldwide.

In 2018, Garelick co-created, directed, wrote, and produced _[Best. Worst. Weekend. Ever.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best.Worst.Weekend.Ever. "Best.Worst.Weekend.Ever.")_, an eight-episode [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") limited series.

In 2023, Garelick directed _[Murder Mystery 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder\_Mystery\_2 "Murder Mystery 2")_, a Netflix movie starring [Adam Sandler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Sandler "Adam Sandler") and [Jennifer Aniston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Aniston "Jennifer Aniston").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-3)

Garelick directed the 2026 comedy film, _[Rolling Loud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Loud\_(film) "Rolling Loud (film)")_, starring [Owen Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Wilson "Owen Wilson"), [Matt Rife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Rife "Matt Rife"), [Henry Winkler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Winkler "Henry Winkler"), and [Travis Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Scott "Travis Scott").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-4)

### American High

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Garelick&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: American High")]

Main article: [American High (company)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_High_(company) "American High (company)")

In 2017, along with producing partner Will Phelps, Garelick purchased A.V. Zogg School in [Liverpool, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool,_New_York "Liverpool, New York") for $1 million, with the intention of using it as a location to produce three high school-centered feature films at a fraction of what they would normally cost to produce.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5) By using the same location, Garelick believed he could save millions thanks to the high tax incentives offered to shoot in Central New York, coupled with savings in below-the-line production costs.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-6) Under the banner of "American High," Garelick produced two movies: _[Banana Split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana\_Split\_(film) "Banana Split (film)")_ for $1.2 million and _[Holly Slept Over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holly\_Slept\_Over "Holly Slept Over")_ for $500,000.

American High's third film, _[Big Time Adolescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Time\_Adolescence "Big Time Adolescence")_, a [coming-of-age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming-of-age "Coming-of-age")[comedy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_film "Comedy film") starring [Pete Davidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Davidson "Pete Davidson") and [Griffin Gluck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffin_Gluck "Griffin Gluck"), was a critical success. After it was screened at the [2019 Sundance Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Sundance_Film_Festival "2019 Sundance Film Festival"), the film's rights were sold to [Hulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulu "Hulu"). The streaming service and American High subsequently signed an eight-movie licensing deal.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5)

Garelick subsequently produced the American High films _[Looks That Kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looks\_That\_Kill\_(film) "Looks That Kill (film)")_, _[The Ultimate Playlist of Noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ultimate\_Playlist\_of\_Noise "The Ultimate Playlist of Noise")_, and _[Plan B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan\_B\_(2021\_film) "Plan B (2021 film)")_. In August 2020, Garelick made his American High directorial debut with _[The Binge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Binge "The Binge")_, a spoof of _[The Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Purge "The Purge")_ set in a world in which drugs and alcohol are illegal, except for one day.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-7) A sequel to the film is set to begin production in January 2022.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5) Four additional American High movies are currently in post-production.

In 2020, Garelick was named one of _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_'s Top Innovators in 2020 for his role in creating American High.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-8) In order to have the area around the A.V. Zogg School zoned for filming by the city of Liverpool, American High also offered a trade school, in addition to its use as a film studio. Each American High production employs about ten students from local colleges like [Syracuse University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_University "Syracuse University"), [Ithaca College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ithaca_College "Ithaca College"), and [Le Moyne College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Moyne_College "Le Moyne College").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5)

In August 2020, Garelick said that American High would relocate, citing high expenditures and code-compliance "confusion."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-9) However, as of 2026, American High is still in operation at A.V. Zogg School.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-10)

# Bat-Mitzvah Girl

By [Emma Allen](https://www.newyorker.com/contributors/emma-allen)

September 4, 2023

![Image 3: A Gen Xer Goes BatMitzvahDress Shopping](https://media.newyorker.com/photos/64f294f986ea71c8f094525d/master/w_2560%2Cc_limit/230911_r42922illu.jpg)

Illustration by João Fazenda

Save this story

Save this story

The 2005 young-adult novel “You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah,” by Fiona Rosenbloom, a pen name of Amanda Stern, recounts the falling-out of two best friends, Stacy Friedman and Lydia Katz, over an unworthy boy, and Stacy’s quest to perform three mitzvahs before her bat mitzvah in order to make things right. It was updated and adapted (more texting, wokeness, lip filler) into a new Adam Sandler movie featuring his two daughters. The other day, Stern stopped by Bloomingdale’s to shop for the perfect bat-mitzvah dress for the bat mitzvah she never had. The store’s “Barbie”-themed window display promised “Best party ever!”

“So, we’re thirteen,” Stern, who is several decades past thirteen, riffed, perusing the racks. “You’re my bestie. You’re my moral support sitting in the front row.”

The hypothetical bestie pulled out a ruched lime-green minidress.

“Green is not for us,” Stern said. “Could my bat-mitzvah theme be Taylor Swift? Is that what the thirteen-year-olds like?”

Unlike her book’s protagonists, who live in Westchester, Stern grew up in Manhattan and attended the Nightingale-Bamford School, on the Upper East Side—“I spent four years working on getting kicked out and I succeeded”—and then Friends Seminary, downtown. In high school, she co-wrote and acted in a play, “Sometimes I Wake Up in the Middle of the Night,” which was produced Off Broadway. It was “about the trials and very rare tribulations of being a teen-ager in New York City,” she said.

She refocussed on her imaginary-party planning. “All right—theme, theme, theme. Oh, the nineties!” She fingered some black Ganni slingbacks, and ruefully noted, “These aren’t nineties.” She continued, “I guess I’d have to get fancy Doc Marten boots, if that exists.”

“I’m Generation X,” she said. “When I was growing up, the bat mitzvahs didn’t have themes. The theme for the bat mitzvah was bat mitzvah. The biggest thing was what we were going to wear.” At Bloomingdale’s, she wore a T-shirt, cutoffs, and pale-pink studded ankle boots. A tiny dog in a frilly dress walked by (accompanied by two actual teens). “I could wear that, but it’s currently being worn by someone cuter,” Stern said.

[![Image 4: Three superheroes. One has super strength one can travel between dimensions and one can remember all six digits of...](https://media.newyorker.com/cartoons/64f29502e58fca21cf25016e/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/230911_a26903.jpg)](https://www.newyorker.com/cartoon/a26903)

She recalled the first bat mitzvah she attended. “I was a really awkward, funny-looking kid,” she said. “And I somehow decided that a sweaterdress would make me pretty.” Hers was a heather-gray turtleneck—“I was sixty pounds. It just hung on me.” When she arrived at the temple, “I was one of forty-seven girls wearing sweaterdresses. It was so deflating.”

Video From The New Yorker

[Bernie Sanders Takes on Data Centers | The New Yorker Radio Hour](https://www.newyorker.com/video/watch/the-new-yorker-interview-radio-hour-bernie-sanders-interview)

No closer to finding The Dress, she sat down at Studio 59, the Bloomingdale’s bar, ordered hummus, and explained that she’d rewritten parts of the book for its recent reprinting: “I started reading through it and I was, like, ‘Yeah, this is problematic.’” Stacy’s fat (and bullied) younger brother is now a gawky genius. Stacy implores God for: “More follows on TikTok. An Oculus Quest headset. World peace.” Gone are the Sean John backpacks and Seven jeans. With the help of a friend’s thirteen-year-old, Stern added some contemporary lingo: “cap,” “ship.”

She described her own four-girl middle-school clique: “We were all BFFs,” she said. Two were Jewish. Two were not. “That was never a big deal,” she said—until, in seventh grade, students were given the option of taking a Jewish holiday off. The Jewish girls showed up at school; the goyim went to the movies without them.

“_Betrayal_,” Stern said. “It was the biggest fight I think I’ve ever had in my life. It ended up with one of the moviegoers slapping me across the face in front of the entire class. She slapped me because I called her—this is unprintable—I called her a ‘cock-sucking dyke,’ which totally makes sense.” The girls reconciled. “She is one of my best friends to this day,” Stern said. One of the other friends, she added, eventually “taught me about puberty and how to give a blow job, and she put a tampon in me, which was too confusing—it was parallel parking when you can’t see over the steering wheel.”

In addition to a new novel for adults and a newsletter “for those who want to live more easily in a world that often feels too hard,” Stern is currently working on an online course for parents of anxious kids. Her top advice: “Don’t lie to them.”

Stern Googled “nineties fashion dress” and pulled up images of spaghetti-strap frocks over white T-shirts. “That’s it!” she said. “That is what they used to call a baby tee.” She hit the racks again and pulled out a diminutive T-shirt with a young devil in a Martini glass and the words “_BORN TO RAISE HELL_” on it ($150). Free People had some spaghetti-strap dresses, including a navy one with a floral pattern, on sale for $76.80. Stern held up the ensemble and admired her handiwork.“That was a little stressful!” she said. “But we persevered, and it paid off.”♦

Paul John Weitz(/waɪts/; born November 19, 1965) is an American screenwriter, director and producer. He is the older brother of filmmaker Chris Weitz. Together they worked on the comedy films American Pie and About a Boy; for the latter, they were both nominated for the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay.Weitz is also a writer, executive producer, and director of the Amazon Prime Video dramedy series Mozart in the Jungle. ×

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American film director and screenwriter (born 1965)

| Paul Weitz |
| --- |
| [![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Paul_Weitz_at_2015_Sundance_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Paul_Weitz_at_2015_Sundance_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Weitz_at_2015_Sundance_(cropped).jpg) Weitz in 2015 |
| Born | Paul John Weitz (1965-11-19) November 19, 1965 (age 60) [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), U.S. |
| Education | [Wesleyan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_University "Wesleyan University") |

| Notable work | * _[American Pie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Pie\_(film) "American Pie (film)")_ * _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_ * _[Mozart in the Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart\_in\_the\_Jungle "Mozart in the Jungle")_ |
| Spouse | Patricia Brown ​ (m.2001)​ |
| Children | 3 |

**Paul John Weitz** ([/w aɪ t s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born November 19, 1965) is an American screenwriter, director and producer. He is the older brother of filmmaker [Chris Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz "Chris Weitz"). Together they worked on the comedy films _[American Pie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Pie\_(film) "American Pie (film)")_ and _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_; for the latter, they were both nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-1) Weitz is also a writer, executive producer, and director of the [Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video") dramedy series _[Mozart in the Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart\_in\_the\_Jungle "Mozart in the Jungle")_.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Weitz was born in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), the son of actress [Susan Kohner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Kohner "Susan Kohner") and Berlin-born novelist/menswear designer [John Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Weitz "John Weitz").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-2) His brother is filmmaker [Chris Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz "Chris Weitz"). Weitz is the grandson of Bohemian-born ([Austrian-Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian-Jewish "Austrian-Jewish")) agent and producer [Paul Kohner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kohner "Paul Kohner") and actress [Lupita Tovar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lupita_Tovar "Lupita Tovar") on his maternal side.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTGrow-4) Tovar, who was from [Oaxaca City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oaxaca_City "Oaxaca City"), Mexico,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTimes-ABetterLife-2010-5) starred in _[Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa\_(1932\_film) "Santa (1932 film)")_, [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")'s first [talkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talkie "Talkie"), in 1932, as well as a Mexican version of _[Drácula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula\_(1931\_Spanish-language\_film) "Dracula (1931 Spanish-language film)")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NPR-6) Weitz' paternal grandparents, who were Jewish, escaped [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"), where his grandfather had been a successful textile manufacturer, and family intimates of [Christopher Isherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Isherwood "Christopher Isherwood") and [Marlene Dietrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dietrich "Marlene Dietrich").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTGrow-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-JJWeitz-7)

Weitz's father and maternal grandfather were [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-11) whereas his maternal grandmother was [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic"). He was raised in a nonreligious household.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-JJWeitz-7)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-InterfaithFamily-Inglourious-2009-12)

Weitz attended the [Allen-Stevenson School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen-Stevenson_School "Allen-Stevenson School") with his brother and [Collegiate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_School_(New_York) "Collegiate School (New York)"). In 1988, he graduated from [Wesleyan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_University "Wesleyan University").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Wesleyan-NotableAlumni-13) While at Wesleyan, Weitz studied under film instructor [Jeanine Basinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanine_Basinger "Jeanine Basinger").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-HartfordCourant-Basinger-2002-14)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early career")]

Weitz' early career involved many collaborations with his brother.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-1of3-2011-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-2of3-2011-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-3of3-2011-17) Some of the work they have done as screenwriters has been both credited and uncredited.[[18]

**Christopher John Weitz** ([/w aɪ t s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born November 30, 1969) is an American filmmaker and actor. He is best known for his work with his brother [Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker) "Paul Weitz (filmmaker)") on the comedy films _[American Pie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Pie\_(film) "American Pie (film)")_ and _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_; the latter earned the Weitz brothers a nomination for the [Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-NYTimes-WeitzBros-2015-1) Among his other main works, Weitz was one of the lead actors in the [Miguel Arteta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Arteta "Miguel Arteta")-directed film _[Chuck & Buck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck\_&\_Buck "Chuck & Buck")_, directed [the film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Golden_Compass_(film) "The Golden Compass (film)") of the novel _[The Golden Compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Golden\_Compass "The Golden Compass")_ and the [film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Saga:_New_Moon "The Twilight Saga: New Moon") of _[New Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Moon\_(novel) "New Moon (novel)")_ from the series of _[Twilight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight\_(novel\_series) "Twilight (novel series)")_ books, wrote the screenplay for Disney's 2015 live-action adaptation of _[Cinderella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinderella\_(2015\_American\_film) "Cinderella (2015 American film)")_, and co-wrote _[Rogue One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogue\_One "Rogue One")_ with [Tony Gilroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Gilroy "Tony Gilroy") and _[Antz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antz "Antz")_ with [Todd Alcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todd_Alcott "Todd Alcott") and Paul.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chris_Weitz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Weitz was born in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), the son of actress [Susan Kohner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Kohner "Susan Kohner") and Berlin-born novelist/menswear designer [John Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Weitz "John Weitz").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-NYTimes-JohnWeitz-Obit-2002-2) His brother is filmmaker [Paul Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker) "Paul Weitz (filmmaker)"). Weitz is the grandson of [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_people "Czech people")-born agent and producer [Paul Kohner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kohner "Paul Kohner") and actress [Lupita Tovar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lupita_Tovar "Lupita Tovar") on his maternal side.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-LATimes-ABetterLife-2011-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-NYTimes-GrowingUpWeitz-2000-4) Tovar, who was from [Oaxaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oaxaca,_Oaxaca "Oaxaca, Oaxaca"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-NYTimes-ABetterLife-2010-5) starred in _[Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa\_(1932\_film) "Santa (1932 film)")_, [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")'s first [talkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talkie "Talkie"), in 1932, as well as a Spanish language version of _[Drácula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula\_(1931\_Spanish-language\_film) "Dracula (1931 Spanish-language film)")._[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-NPR-FreshAir-DirectorsWeitz-2002-6) Weitz' paternal grandparents escaped [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"), before which his grandfather was a successful textile manufacturer, with the family being intimates of writer [Christopher Isherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Isherwood "Christopher Isherwood") and actress [Marlene Dietrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dietrich "Marlene Dietrich").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-NYTimes-GrowingUpWeitz-2000-4)

Weitz's father and maternal grandfather were [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz#cite_note-NYTimes-WeitzBrothers-2015-7)[[8]](

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Young adult fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Young_adult_fiction&redirect=no "Young adult fiction"))

Literature written for adolescents and young adults

"Juvenile fiction" redirects here. For children's fiction, see [Children's literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_literature "Children's literature").

**Young adult literature** (**YA**) is literature written for readers aged 12 to 18.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-2) It may include themes found in adult fiction, such as [family dysfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysfunctional_family "Dysfunctional family"), substance abuse, alcoholism, and sexuality.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-Wells-3)

The earliest known use of term _young adult_ occurred in 1942.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-4) Librarians developed the category of young adult literature to help bridge the gap between [children's literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_literature "Children's literature") and adult literature.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-5) According to a study conducted in 2023, 55% of young adult literature consumers were over 18 years of age. 78% of adult consumers purchased with the intent to read themselves. Of these adult buyers, 51% were between ages 30 and 44.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-6) This highlights the fact that readers of young adult literature are often adults.

## Definitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Young_adult_literature&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Definitions")]

According to author and academic [Michael Cart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cart "Michael Cart"), the term young adult literature "first found common usage in the late 1960s, in reference to realistic fiction that was set in the real (as opposed to imagined), contemporary world and addressed problems, issues, and life circumstances of interest to young readers aged approximately 12–18". However, "The term 'young adult literature' is inherently amorphous, for its constituent terms 'young adult' and 'literature' are dynamic, changing as culture and society — which provide their context — change",[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-7) and "even those who study and teach it have not reached a consensus on a definition".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-8)

Victor Malo-Juvera and Crag Hill, in "The Young Adult Canon: A Literary Solar System", note that in 2019 there was no consensus on the definition of young adult literature and list a number of definitions, including:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction#cite_note-9)

*   Books that readers aged 12 to 20 chose independently
*   Literature written for young people aged 11 to 18 and books marked as "young adult" by a publisher
*   Literature including a teenager who is the main character and who, as the center of the plot, engages in problems related to and relatable to the lives of teenagers
*   Novels told by "a teen protagonist speaking from an adolescent point of view, with all the limitations of understanding that implies"

This provides an overall consensus in the literary world that the definition of young adult literature is unique to the author, reader, and publisher. There are common themes and tropes seen across young adult literary work that lead a piece to be classified as young adult literature as a general classification with some aspects that may fall into adult literature as well as children's literature.

_**You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah**_ is a 2023 American [coming-of-age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_of_age_film "Coming of age film")[comedy-drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy-drama "Comedy-drama") film directed by [Sammi Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen "Sammi Cohen"), written by Alison Peck, and produced by [Adam Sandler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Sandler "Adam Sandler"), [Tim Herlihy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Herlihy "Tim Herlihy"), [Leslie Morgenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Morgenstein "Leslie Morgenstein"), and [Elysa Koplovitz Dutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elysa_Dutton "Elysa Dutton"). Based on the 2005 [young adult novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_adult_fiction "Young adult fiction") of the same name, the film stars Sandler and his wife, Jackie Sandler, as well as their daughters, [Sadie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadie_Sandler "Sadie Sandler") and [Sunny Sandler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Sandler "Sunny Sandler"). It also stars [Samantha Lorraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samantha_Lorraine "Samantha Lorraine"), [Idina Menzel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idina_Menzel "Idina Menzel"), Dylan Hoffman, [Sarah Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Sherman "Sarah Sherman"), Dan Bulla, [Ido Mosseri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ido_Mosseri "Ido Mosseri"), [Jackie Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Hoffman "Jackie Hoffman"), and [Luis Guzmán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Guzm%C3%A1n "Luis Guzmán"). It tells the story of two best friends whose [bat mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_and_bat_mitzvah "Bar and bat mitzvah") plans go awry as they fight for the attention of the same popular boy.

Produced by [Happy Madison Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Madison_Productions "Happy Madison Productions") and [Alloy Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy_Entertainment "Alloy Entertainment"), the film was released by [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") on August 25, 2023.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah#cite_note-2)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Stacy Friedman dreams about her upcoming _[bat mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar\_and\_bat\_mitzvah "Bar and bat mitzvah")_, including sharing it with her best friend Lydia Rodriguez Katz, and sharing a dance with her crush, Andy Goldfarb. She clashes with her parents, Bree and Danny, over planning the "perfect" party, which she believes will determine her future.

When popular student Kym Chang Cohen invites Lydia to her house, Stacy tags along. The girls go on a high ledge, where Andy and his friends meet up with them. On a dare and to impress Andy, Stacy agrees to jump off the ledge into the water below. Enjoying Andy's and everyone's approval is short-lived, as Stacy's bloody maxi-pad floats up next to her. Angry that everyone, including Lydia, is laughing at her, Stacy "calls it", and Lydia announces the time that she lost her crush on Andy.

Once school starts, Stacy learns that Lydia and Andy are dating. Feeling betrayed, she stops talking to her and sends a text message to an anonymous group that Lydia has long hair on her nipples. Stacy even sabotages an entrance video she had been making for Lydia's upcoming _bat mitzvah_ with humiliating personal video clips. However, she does not plan to send it.

Stacy continues trying to get Andy's attention, so she visits his grandmother's retirement home, and pretends to be a volunteer. She tries to look older and more popular, and argues with her parents over planning her _bat mitzvah_. Andy eventually offers to give Stacy her first kiss. Hiding behind the curtains of a [Torah ark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torah_ark "Torah ark"), they are interrupted by their teacher Rabbi Rebecca, which leads to more fighting between her and her father.

Lydia's mother Gabi, unaware Stacy and Lydia are fighting, arrives at the Friedman's, and asks Bree for the entrance video for Lydia's _bat mitzvah_. Not realizing what the video contains, Bree sends it to her. At Lydia's _bat mitzvah_, the hateful entrance video is played. Although Stacy tries to get the video stopped, the damage is done. As Lydia walks into her party, she runs off and angrily chastises Stacy.

At Stacy's bat mitzvah day, she starts to [read from the Torah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torah_reading "Torah reading") from her _[parsha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsha "Parsha")_ of [Ki Tissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ki_Tissa "Ki Tissa"). Seeing that Lydia and her parents are missing, she stops, then confesses everything to the audience. She berates Andy for his bad behavior and for driving her and Lydia apart. She then finishes her Torah reading at her father's urging.

Afterwards, Stacy runs through town to apologize to Lydia and invites her to her party later that night. When Lydia and her parents arrive, they are surprised that Stacy has made it into a party for Lydia, too, and the girls make up. Stacy starts dancing with Matteo, a foreign classmate who has been interested in her.

Sometime later, Stacy, Lydia, and their friends have a bake sale to help the retirement home.

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reception")]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 91% of 80 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 6.8/10.The website's consensus reads: "A coming-of-age comedy that sidesteps simple nostalgia, _You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah_ finds fresh humor in adolescent anxiety—and suggests a bright future for star Sunny Sandler."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes-9)[Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which uses a [weighted average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_arithmetic_mean "Weighted arithmetic mean"), assigned the film a score of 71 out of 100, based on 20 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Are_So_Not_Invited_to_My_Bat_Mitzvah#cite_note-Metacritic-10)

**Jeremy Garelick** (born November 30, 1975) is an American screenwriter, director, and producer.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Garelick&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Garelick was born in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). He attended [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") and graduated in Film Studies.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-1) He is of [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish") background.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-2)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Garelick&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

After graduating from college, Garelick began his career working as an assistant in [Creative Artists Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Artists_Agency "Creative Artists Agency")'s Motion Picture Literary department. He served as the assistant to director [Joel Schumacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Schumacher "Joel Schumacher") on _[Tigerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigerland "Tigerland")_, _[Bad Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad\_Company\_(2002\_film) "Bad Company (2002 film)")_, _[Phone Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phone\_Booth\_(film) "Phone Booth (film)")_, and _[The Phantom of the Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phantom\_of\_the\_Opera\_(2004\_film) "The Phantom of the Opera (2004 film)")_. He was the second unit director on Schumacher’s 2003 movie _[\_Veronica Guerin\_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veronica\_Guerin\_(film) "Veronica Guerin (film)")_.

While working on Veronica Guerin in 2002, Garelick sold _The Golden Tux_, a spec script he co-wrote with Todd Phillips, to [Dimension Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension_Films "Dimension Films"). The script caught the attention of [Vince Vaughn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Vaughn "Vince Vaughn"), who brought Garelick in to co-write and co-produce _[The Break-Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Break-Up "The Break-Up")_.

After the commercial success of _The Break-Up_, Garelick worked with Phillips again on an uncredited re-write of _[The Hangover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hangover "The Hangover")_. The film was a major critical and commercial success, making over $465 million at the box office.

Garelick’s early career came full circle in 2013, when he was hired by [Screen Gems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Gems "Screen Gems") to direct and produce _[The Wedding Ringer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wedding\_Ringer "The Wedding Ringer")_, a feature film that evolved from _The Golden Tux_. Despite negative critical reviews, the film was a box-office success when it premiered in 2015, grossing over $79 million worldwide.

In 2018, Garelick co-created, directed, wrote, and produced _[Best. Worst. Weekend. Ever.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best.Worst.Weekend.Ever. "Best.Worst.Weekend.Ever.")_, an eight-episode [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") limited series.

In 2023, Garelick directed _[Murder Mystery 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder\_Mystery\_2 "Murder Mystery 2")_, a Netflix movie starring [Adam Sandler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Sandler "Adam Sandler") and [Jennifer Aniston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Aniston "Jennifer Aniston").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-3)

Garelick directed the 2026 comedy film, _[Rolling Loud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Loud\_(film) "Rolling Loud (film)")_, starring [Owen Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Wilson "Owen Wilson"), [Matt Rife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Rife "Matt Rife"), [Henry Winkler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Winkler "Henry Winkler"), and [Travis Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Scott "Travis Scott").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-4)

### American High

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeremy_Garelick&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: American High")]

Main article: [American High (company)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_High_(company) "American High (company)")

In 2017, along with producing partner Will Phelps, Garelick purchased A.V. Zogg School in [Liverpool, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool,_New_York "Liverpool, New York") for $1 million, with the intention of using it as a location to produce three high school-centered feature films at a fraction of what they would normally cost to produce.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5) By using the same location, Garelick believed he could save millions thanks to the high tax incentives offered to shoot in Central New York, coupled with savings in below-the-line production costs.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-6) Under the banner of "American High," Garelick produced two movies: _[Banana Split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana\_Split\_(film) "Banana Split (film)")_ for $1.2 million and _[Holly Slept Over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holly\_Slept\_Over "Holly Slept Over")_ for $500,000.

American High's third film, _[Big Time Adolescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Time\_Adolescence "Big Time Adolescence")_, a [coming-of-age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming-of-age "Coming-of-age")[comedy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_film "Comedy film") starring [Pete Davidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Davidson "Pete Davidson") and [Griffin Gluck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffin_Gluck "Griffin Gluck"), was a critical success. After it was screened at the [2019 Sundance Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Sundance_Film_Festival "2019 Sundance Film Festival"), the film's rights were sold to [Hulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulu "Hulu"). The streaming service and American High subsequently signed an eight-movie licensing deal.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5)

Garelick subsequently produced the American High films _[Looks That Kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looks\_That\_Kill\_(film) "Looks That Kill (film)")_, _[The Ultimate Playlist of Noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ultimate\_Playlist\_of\_Noise "The Ultimate Playlist of Noise")_, and _[Plan B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan\_B\_(2021\_film) "Plan B (2021 film)")_. In August 2020, Garelick made his American High directorial debut with _[The Binge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Binge "The Binge")_, a spoof of _[The Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Purge "The Purge")_ set in a world in which drugs and alcohol are illegal, except for one day.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-7) A sequel to the film is set to begin production in January 2022.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5) Four additional American High movies are currently in post-production.

In 2020, Garelick was named one of _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_'s Top Innovators in 2020 for his role in creating American High.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-8) In order to have the area around the A.V. Zogg School zoned for filming by the city of Liverpool, American High also offered a trade school, in addition to its use as a film studio. Each American High production employs about ten students from local colleges like [Syracuse University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_University "Syracuse University"), [Ithaca College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ithaca_College "Ithaca College"), and [Le Moyne College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Moyne_College "Le Moyne College").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-NYT-5)

In August 2020, Garelick said that American High would relocate, citing high expenditures and code-compliance "confusion."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-9) However, as of 2026, American High is still in operation at A.V. Zogg School.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Garelick#cite_note-10)

**Paul John Weitz** ([/w aɪ t s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born November 19, 1965) is an American screenwriter, director and producer. He is the older brother of filmmaker [Chris Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz "Chris Weitz"). Together they worked on the comedy films _[American Pie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Pie\_(film) "American Pie (film)")_ and _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_; for the latter, they were both nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-1) Weitz is also a writer, executive producer, and director of the [Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video") dramedy series _[Mozart in the Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozart\_in\_the\_Jungle "Mozart in the Jungle")_.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Weitz was born in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), the son of actress [Susan Kohner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Kohner "Susan Kohner") and Berlin-born novelist/menswear designer [John Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Weitz "John Weitz").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-2) His brother is filmmaker [Chris Weitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Weitz "Chris Weitz"). Weitz is the grandson of Bohemian-born ([Austrian-Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian-Jewish "Austrian-Jewish")) agent and producer [Paul Kohner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kohner "Paul Kohner") and actress [Lupita Tovar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lupita_Tovar "Lupita Tovar") on his maternal side.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTGrow-4) Tovar, who was from [Oaxaca City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oaxaca_City "Oaxaca City"), Mexico,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTimes-ABetterLife-2010-5) starred in _[Santa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa\_(1932\_film) "Santa (1932 film)")_, [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")'s first [talkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talkie "Talkie"), in 1932, as well as a Mexican version of _[Drácula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula\_(1931\_Spanish-language\_film) "Dracula (1931 Spanish-language film)")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NPR-6) Weitz' paternal grandparents, who were Jewish, escaped [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"), where his grandfather had been a successful textile manufacturer, and family intimates of [Christopher Isherwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Isherwood "Christopher Isherwood") and [Marlene Dietrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dietrich "Marlene Dietrich").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTGrow-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-JJWeitz-7)

Weitz's father and maternal grandfather were [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-11) whereas his maternal grandmother was [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic"). He was raised in a nonreligious household.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-JJWeitz-7)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-InterfaithFamily-Inglourious-2009-12)

Weitz attended the [Allen-Stevenson School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen-Stevenson_School "Allen-Stevenson School") with his brother and [Collegiate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_School_(New_York) "Collegiate School (New York)"). In 1988, he graduated from [Wesleyan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_University "Wesleyan University").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Wesleyan-NotableAlumni-13) While at Wesleyan, Weitz studied under film instructor [Jeanine Basinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanine_Basinger "Jeanine Basinger").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-HartfordCourant-Basinger-2002-14)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early career")]

Weitz' early career involved many collaborations with his brother.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-1of3-2011-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-2of3-2011-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-3of3-2011-17) Some of the work they have done as screenwriters has been both credited and uncredited.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-18)

Weitz began his film career as a co-writer on the 1998 animated film _[Antz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antz "Antz")_. He followed this with work on various sitcoms such as _[Off Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off\_Centre "Off Centre")_ and [the 1998 revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Island_(1998_TV_series) "Fantasy Island (1998 TV series)") of [the 1977 series _Fantasy Island_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Island "Fantasy Island"). In 1999, he and Chris directed and produced _[American Pie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Pie\_(film) "American Pie (film)")_, which was written by [Adam Herz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Herz "Adam Herz"), and became a major box office success. Weitz returned as executive producer on the film's two theatrical sequels.

In 2002, the Weitz brothers co-wrote and co-directed _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_, the [Hugh Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Grant "Hugh Grant") film based on the book by [Nick Hornby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hornby "Nick Hornby").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-LosAngeles-AAB-2002-20) The film was originally set up at [New Line Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Line_Cinema "New Line Cinema") with [Robert De Niro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_De_Niro "Robert De Niro") producing, and the main character as an American. The brothers felt that it was important that the character is British. Inspiration came from the film _[The Apartment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Apartment "The Apartment")_ (1960). They were nominated for an [Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Adapted_Screenplay "Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NPR-6)

Weitz has written and directed the well-received romantic comedy _[In Good Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Good\_Company\_(2004\_film) "In Good Company (2004 film)")_ and the political satire _[American Dreamz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Dreamz "American Dreamz")_, which faced mixed reviews. Additional writing credits include the television show _Cracking Up_.

He has also directed an adaptation of [Darren Shan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darren_Shan "Darren Shan")'s young adult novel _[Cirque du Freak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirque\_du\_Freak "Cirque du Freak")_ called _[The Vampire's Assistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Vampire's\_Assistant\_(film) "The Vampire's Assistant (film)")_. He directed the film _[Little Fockers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Fockers "Little Fockers")_ (2010), the sequel to _[Meet the Parents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meet\_the\_Parents "Meet the Parents")_ and _[Meet the Fockers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meet\_the\_Fockers "Meet the Fockers")_.

Subsequently he wrote and directed _[Being Flynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Being\_Flynn "Being Flynn")_, an adaptation of [Nick Flynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Flynn "Nick Flynn")'s memoir _[Another Bullshit Night in Suck City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another\_Bullshit\_Night\_in\_Suck\_City "Another Bullshit Night in Suck City")_, starring [Robert De Niro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_De_Niro "Robert De Niro").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-2of3-2011-16) Weitz said he worked collaboratively with Flynn to translate the dense original source material into its film adaptation.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-3of3-2011-17)

Weitz also directed the movie _[Admission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admission\_(2013\_film) "Admission (2013 film)")_, starring [Tina Fey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tina_Fey "Tina Fey").

### _Grandma_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Grandma")]

In 2015, Weitz directed the film, _[Grandma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandma\_(2015\_film) "Grandma (2015 film)")_, which starred [Lily Tomlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lily_Tomlin "Lily Tomlin").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTGma-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-LATGma-23) The film premiered at the [2015 Sundance Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Sundance_Film_Festival "2015 Sundance Film Festival") on January 30, as the closing night film.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Deadline-Grandma-Sundance-2015-24) The film was Tomlin's first leading role in 27 years, after co-starring with [Bette Midler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bette_Midler "Bette Midler") in the comedy film _[Big Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Business\_(1988\_film) "Big Business (1988 film)")_ (1988). It is the second collaboration between Tomlin and Weitz, who previously directed her in his film _[Admission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admission\_(2013\_film) "Admission (2013 film)")_ (2013).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-LATGma-23) The film was released on August 21, 2015, by [Sony Pictures Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Pictures_Classics "Sony Pictures Classics").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Deadline-SPC-Aquires-2015-25)

Weitz had the story idea for many years, but it never fully formed until he met and worked with Tomlin on _Admission_,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-NYTGma-21) saying that "After meeting Lily, the voice and the character really clicked, I had thought about it for years, so I had a lot of it worked out in my head, and then I just went to a coffee shop and wrote it longhand."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-LATGma-23)

Weitz said the film cost under $600,000 to make.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-CharlieRose-Grandma-2015-26) It was well received.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-HReporter-Grandma-Sundance-2015-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Guardian-Grandma-Sundance-2015-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Variety-Grandma-Sundance-2015-29)

### In development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: In development")]

Weitz has a production company with his brother Chris Weitz and producer Andrew Miano called Depth of Field. In March 2016, Weitz and his brother signed a two-year first look deal with [Amazon Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Studios "Amazon Studios").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Wrap-AmazonDeal-2016-30)

*   A live-action adaptation of [Michael Moorcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Moorcock "Michael Moorcock")'s [Elric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elric "Elric") saga, which his brother Chris said he enjoyed as a child. Weitz's Depth of Field production company was meant to create the films as a potential trilogy for [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures"). In a May 2007 interview with _[Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire\_(magazine) "Empire (magazine)")_ magazine Weitz's brother announced that he had met with Moorcock, who trusted him with the films, and described his wish for Paul to direct the film.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Empire-Moorcock-Elric-2007-31)
*   _Shield of Straw_ – producing an English remake of the 2013 Japanese action thriller, _[Shield of Straw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shield\_of\_Straw "Shield of Straw")_[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Variety-ShieldofStraw-2015-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Deadline-ShieldofStraw-2015-33)
*   _Ghost Train_ – producing a remake of the 2006 Japanese horror film, _Soul Reviver_[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Variety-ShieldofStraw-2015-32)
*   _[Birthright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthright\_(2010\_film) "Birthright (2010 film)")_ – producing a remake of the 2010 Japanese thriller[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Variety-ShieldofStraw-2015-32)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-Variety-Birthright-2014-34)
*   _Sinatoro_ – producing a TV series with [Grant Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Morrison "Grant Morrison") for [Universal Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Television "Universal Television")[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-HReporter-Sinatoro-2016-35)

## Playwright

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Playwright")]

While in college at Wesleyan, Weitz wrote the play _Mango Tea_, which was performed [Off-Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-Broadway "Off-Broadway").

Weitz has written a number of plays, including _Roulette_, _Privilege_, _Show People_ and _Trust_, all of which have been produced Off-Broadway in New York City.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-LortelArchives-36)_Trust_ starred [Zach Braff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zach_Braff "Zach Braff"), [Bobby Cannavale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Cannavale "Bobby Cannavale"), [Sutton Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Foster "Sutton Foster"), and [Ari Graynor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ari_Graynor "Ari Graynor"), and was directed by Peter DuBois at [Second Stage Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Stage_Theatre "Second Stage Theatre"). It will be produced in Brazil, Germany and Greece in 2013[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]. In 2012, Second Stage, which had previously produced _Privilege_ and _Show People_, produced _Lonely, I'm Not_, a new comedy by Weitz starring [Topher Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topher_Grace "Topher Grace") and [Olivia Thirlby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivia_Thirlby "Olivia Thirlby"). _Lonely, I'm Not_ was a _New York Times_ critics pick.

As a writer, Weitz has discussed semi-jokingly the fact that he avoids the discomfort in his life by turning to the act of writing.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-2of3-2011-16) He sees a good play structure as being very different from a good film structure, and thinks that it is rare for plays as source material to be easily adapted into film.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)#cite_note-WGAw-WeitzBros-3of3-2011-17)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paul_Weitz_(filmmaker)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In 2001, Weitz married novelist Patricia Brown, with whom he has three children.

**Sammi Cohen** (born 1988 or 1989)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-HuffPost_2022-1) is an American film and television director. They directed the 2017 comedy series _[Hollywood Darlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood\_Darlings "Hollywood Darlings")_ for [Pop TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_(American_TV_channel) "Pop (American TV channel)"), and the [coming-of-age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming-of-age "Coming-of-age") films _[Crush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crush\_(2022\_film) "Crush (2022 film)")_ (2022) and _[You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You\_Are\_So\_Not\_Invited\_to\_My\_Bat\_Mitzvah "You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah")_ (2023).

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sammi_Cohen&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

Before becoming a director, Cohen worked as an [editor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_editing "Video editing") and [visual effects supervisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_effects_supervisor "Visual effects supervisor") on [commercials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercials "Commercials") and [music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_videos "Music videos").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-2) Cohen's directorial career began when they filmed [comedy music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_music "Comedy music") videos of their friends at [Upright Citizens Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upright_Citizens_Brigade_Theatre "Upright Citizens Brigade Theatre"), and were then hired to direct original content for [CollegeHumor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CollegeHumor "CollegeHumor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-3) They were the director of _[Hollywood Darlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood\_Darlings "Hollywood Darlings")_ on [Pop TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_(American_TV_channel) "Pop (American TV channel)"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-4) and they directed series for [YouTube Originals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_Originals "YouTube Originals") and [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:3-5) They have also directed commercials.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-6)

In July 2021, it was reported that Cohen would direct [_Crush_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crush_(2022_film) "Crush (2022 film)") (then called _Love in Color_) for [Hulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulu "Hulu"). A queer [romance film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_film "Romance film") set in a [high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_school "High school"), the film was Cohen's feature debut.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:2-7)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:3-5) Cohen said they were attracted to the project because it was a queer narrative "where the story isn't about [coming out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out")", and they sought to work on the "kind of movie that I really desperately needed growing up".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-HuffPost_2022-1)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:3-5)_Crush_, starring [Rowan Blanchard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowan_Blanchard "Rowan Blanchard") and [Auliʻi Cravalho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auli%CA%BBi_Cravalho "Auliʻi Cravalho"), was released in April 2022 on Hulu.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-8)

In 2022, [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") announced its development of _[You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You\_Are\_So\_Not\_Invited\_to\_My\_Bat\_Mitzvah "You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah")_, a film adapted from the 2005 [Fiona Rosenbloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Stern "Amanda Stern") novel of the same name. Netflix announced that the film would be directed by Cohen and would star [Adam Sandler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Sandler "Adam Sandler") and his daughters.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-9) Cohen, who was hired because Sandler was looking for a young Jewish director,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-10) was added to the project after the script had been obtained by [Alloy Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alloy_Entertainment "Alloy Entertainment") and Sandler's [Happy Madison Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Madison_Productions "Happy Madison Productions"). Cohen also joined after Sandler's daughters had been cast in leading roles.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-11) In August 2023, _You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah_ was released on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"). In a favorable review, Gary Goldstein of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ wrote that Cohen brought a "more spontaneous, loose-limbed style" to the film.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-12) Discussing their feature films, Cohen said: "With _Crush_, I made a movie for the gays and for the Little Sammies, and then with _Bat Mitzvah_, I was so excited to make a movie for Jewish kids."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-13)

In January 2026, _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ reported that Cohen would direct _Betas_, a comedy film written by [Ilana Wolpert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilana_Wolpert "Ilana Wolpert").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-14)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sammi_Cohen&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Cohen was raised in [Woodland Hills, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland_Hills,_Los_Angeles "Woodland Hills, Los Angeles"), in a [Reform Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Jewish "Reform Jewish") household.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:0-15) They grew up going to temple and celebrating the [High Holy Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Holy_Days "High Holy Days").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:1-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-17) While they attended [Hebrew school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_school "Hebrew school") and had a [bat mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat_mitzvah "Bat mitzvah") party at age 13, they did not do a traditional ceremony.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-19) They officially became a bat mitzvah while on their [birthright trip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthright_trip "Birthright trip") in Israel.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:0-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:1-16) They describe themself as a "very progressive Jew" and their Jewish community as "very progressive".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:0-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-20) They go to [Shabbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabbat "Shabbat") services.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:1-16)

Cohen is [queer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queer "Queer"), [non-binary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-binary_gender "Non-binary gender"), and uses _[they/them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/They/them "They/them")_ pronouns.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-:0-15)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-21) They first came out as nonbinary while performing [stand-up comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedy "Stand-up comedy").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-22) At the 2024 [Independent Spirit Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Spirit_Awards "Independent Spirit Awards"), Cohen and [Zoe Lister-Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoe_Lister-Jones "Zoe Lister-Jones") announced their relationship.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammi_Cohen#cite_note-23)
